A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TTT3R and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite renumbering and the expanded appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original camera-pose, video-depth, and 3D-reconstruction experiments, including benchmark curves, qualitative reconstructions, and appendix Tables 1–2.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds gating, finetuning, and state-reset experiments in Appendices A–B.

M1.justification: The core confidence-gated inference rule remains. Appendix A.2 adds a finetuned variant that applies this rule during training. v4 also explicitly specifies TTT3R + State Reset, but several v1 reconstructions reappear labeled as reset-enabled; this disclosure alone does not establish that reset was newly implemented.

E1.justification: Evaluation coverage remains ScanNet, TUM-dynamics, Sintel, KITTI, Bonn, 7-scene, and in-the-wild reconstruction, including thousands-frame sequences already shown in v1. Added studies change procedures within these tasks. Finetuning uses CUT3R's existing training dataset; no distinct new data domain is identified.

E2.justification: v4 adds STream3R to the retained short-sequence pose and depth comparisons. New controlled comparisons evaluate CUT3R with ScalarLR, ConditionLR, TokenLR, Reset, EMA, and BurnIn. Reset-enabled CUT3R also becomes a comparator for the extreme-length visualizations. These substantially broaden the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: Appendix A introduces gate-only training with the encoder, decoder, and output heads frozen, plus TTT3R finetuning on 4–64-view sequences. It sweeps reset/keyframe intervals and EMA shrinkage rates. Appendix B adds matched reset comparisons and long-sequence metric-depth evaluation on Bonn. Original benchmark protocols are otherwise retained.

E4.justification: v1 lacks the systematic design tests added in v4: learned-gate comparisons, finetuning tradeoffs, reset-period and EMA-rate sensitivity, and keyframe-interval ablations. Appendix B additionally examines failures beyond 1000 frames and whether resetting alleviates them, substantially extending mechanism and robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests for the experiments. The added results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Original benchmark curves and shared entries in v1 Tables 1–2, now v4 Tables 6–7, are unchanged. New results establish substantial additional findings: v4 Table 5 reports 1000-frame TUM ATE of 0.093 with reset versus 0.106 without it; Table 1 shows finetuning lowers ATE but worsens KITTI depth. STream3R also changes short-sequence rankings, achieving TUM ATE 0.026 versus TTT3R's 0.028.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 explicitly defines the summation in Equation 7 as a normalized mean, whereas v1 leaves it as an unqualified sum. This is a limited mathematical specification/correction. The central TTT reformulation and derivations remain, with no new theorem, proof, or formal guarantee.

C1.justification: The headline TTT perspective, training-free gate, approximately twofold pose improvement, and 20-FPS/6-GB claims remain. Section 5 adds the optional reset remedy, while Figure 1 now qualifies the extreme-length demonstration as using reset. This limits attribution of that success to the confidence gate alone.

C2.justification: v1 acknowledges residual forgetting generally. v4 documents failures beyond 1000 frames, connects them to unexplored state distributions, and explains the reset remedy and its use in long-sequence demonstrations. It also interprets learned gates' training-length limitations and the finetuning tradeoff between global alignment and per-view depth accuracy.

D1.justification: v4 supplies consequential missing details: mean aggregation in Equation 7, resetting every 100 frames, chunk alignment through metric camera poses without optimization, and which demonstrations use reset. It also documents frozen components, training sequence lengths, and baseline hyperparameter choices. These materially improve reproducibility; the stated code-access link remains unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work expands to learned/dynamic SLAM systems such as VIPE, VGGT-SLAM, and VGGT-Long, and to scene-specific test-time adaptation through CVD and Test3R. STream3R is also added. These refine the existing positioning rather than replace the paper's central research framing.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v4 adds local associative-memory explanations, expands the discussion, and inserts analysis/reset appendices before the retained results and LLM-use sections. Affiliations and the publication header also change; this is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Five new analysis tables and several gating/reset plots substantially expand the visual presentation. Figure 1 replaces the CUT3R reconstruction with a reset-enabled comparison; v1 Figure 11 is reworked into v4 Figures 14–15 with additional controls. Retained tables gain STream3R rows, and several captions are expanded.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important validation and transparency gaps: Appendices A–B test the gate against learned and simple retention alternatives, expose extreme-length failures, and explain reset behind the strongest demonstrations. Adding reset-enabled CUT3R comparisons makes attribution fairer. These substantially strengthen the paper beyond its largely unchanged benchmark results. Some superiority wording remains too broad: Table 5 gives CUT3R + Reset lower rotation error and KITTI Abs Rel than unreset TTT3R, but this qualification does not outweigh the gains in evidence and reproducibility.
